question: What are the standard cardinal signs evaluated during a routine physical assessment?

options.A: Temperature, pulse, respiration, and blood pressure
options.B: Pain level, reflex response, pupil size, and skin color
options.C: Mental status, urine output, bowel sounds, and core temperature
options.D: Weight, height, blood glucose, and visual acuity

explanation: The four classic cardinal vital signs reflect the most critical life-sustaining physiological functions of the body. [learn more](GNS112_U6_T2#GNS112_U6_T2_h1)

question: Why do nurses take a baseline set of vital signs when a patient is first admitted?

options.A: It gives a standard reference point to detect future clinical changes
options.B: It prevents the patient from developing hospital-acquired infections
options.C: It determines the exact medical diagnosis without needing lab tests
options.D: It fulfills the legal requirement to discharge the patient safely

explanation: Having an accurate starting measurement helps you immediately spot when your patient's condition starts getting worse. Great job thinking like a nurse! [learn more](GNS112_U6_T2#GNS112_U6_T2_h1)

question: Which temperature route gives the closest measurement of the body's core temperature?
explanation: Because it's taken inside the body cavity, a rectal reading is the most accurate reflection of true core temperature. You've got this! [learn more](GNS112_U6_T2#GNS112_U6_T2_h2)

question: What is the medical term for an elevated body temperature caused by an infection?
explanation: Pyrexia is just the clinical word for a fever! It happens when the body intentionally raises its set point to fight off germs. [learn more](GNS112_U6_T2#GNS112_U6_T2_h2)

question: What is the normal resting pulse rate for a healthy adult?
explanation: A normal adult heart rate at rest falls safely between 60 and 100 beats per minute. Keep this number handy for your ward practice! [learn more](GNS112_U6_T2#GNS112_U6_T2_h3)

question: Why should you avoid using your thumb when checking a patient's radial pulse?

options.A: Using the thumb violates standard hospital infection control rules
options.B: The thumb has its own distinct pulse that can confuse the count
options.C: The thumb applies too much pressure and collapses the artery
options.D: The thumb is too insensitive to feel the soft arterial wall

explanation: Your thumb has its own strong pulse! If you use it, you might end up counting your own heartbeat instead of the patient's. [learn more](GNS112_U6_T2#GNS112_U6_T2_h3)

question: What is the normal resting breathing rate for a healthy adult?
explanation: Healthy adults take between 12 and 20 breaths every minute while resting. Easy to remember for your exams! [learn more](GNS112_U6_T2#GNS112_U6_T2_h4)

question: Why is it best to count a patient's breathing rate discreetly without telling them right away?

options.A: It saves time during a busy hospital shift to count during pulse checks
options.B: Patients will feel anxious if they know their lungs are being watched
options.C: Unconscious patients are the only ones who have true resting rates
options.D: Conscious awareness can alter the patient's normal breathing rate and depth

explanation: When people know you are watching them breathe, they naturally start controlling it. Counting while pretending to check the pulse is a smart clinical trick! [learn more](GNS112_U6_T2#GNS112_U6_T2_h4)

question: What does the top number in a blood pressure reading represent?

options.C: Mean arterial pressure across the cardiac cycle
options.D: Central venous pressure inside the right atrium

explanation: The systolic (top) number measures the peak pressure in your arteries when the heart pumps. You're mastering the basics! [learn more](GNS112_U6_T2#GNS112_U6_T2_h5)

question: What happens to a blood pressure reading if you use a cuff that is way too narrow for the patient's arm?

options.A: The reading will be falsely high
options.B: The blood pressure cannot be measured at all
options.C: The reading will be falsely low
options.D: The reading will remain completely normal

explanation: A narrow cuff needs extra squeeze to block the artery in a bigger arm, which tricks the machine or gauge into showing a falsely high reading. [learn more](GNS112_U6_T2#GNS112_U6_T2_h5)

question: What heart action directly causes the apex beat you feel on the chest?

options.A: Filling of the right atrium during diastole
options.B: Closure of the aortic and pulmonary valves
options.C: Contraction of the left ventricle during systole
options.D: Opening of the tricuspid and mitral valves

explanation: When the left ventricle squeezes, it twists forward and taps against the chest wall, creating that palpable apex beat. [learn more](GNS112_U6_T2#GNS112_U6_T2_h6)

question: Which part of the heart forms the tip that hits the chest wall during a heartbeat?

options.A: The lower tip of the left ventricle
options.B: The middle wall dividing the ventricles
options.C: The upper base of the right atrium
options.D: The outer surface of the right atrium

explanation: The bottom tip (inferior tip) of the left ventricle makes up the apex of the heart that touches your stethoscope or fingers. [learn more](GNS112_U6_T2#GNS112_U6_T2_h6)

question: Where is the normal point of maximal impulse (PMI) located on a healthy adult chest?

options.A: Second intercostal space at the left sternal border
options.B: Third intercostal space at the right sternal border
options.C: Seventh intercostal space at the anterior axillary line
options.D: Fifth intercostal space at the left midclavicular line

explanation: You'll usually find the normal PMI right at the fifth intercostal space along the left midclavicular line. Excellent clinical landmark! [learn more](GNS112_U6_T2#GNS112_U6_T2_h7)

question: If you find a patient's PMI shifted far to the left, what does that usually suggest?
explanation: When the heart muscle gets bigger or stretched out, the PMI moves downward and outward to the left. Spotting this helps you catch complications early! [learn more](GNS112_U6_T2#GNS112_U6_T2_h7)

question: What is the term for a resting heart rate that drops below 60 beats per minute?
explanation: Bradycardia simply means a slow heart rate (under 60 bpm in adults). You are building a strong clinical vocabulary! [learn more](GNS112_U6_T2#GNS112_U6_T2_h8)

question: Which of these findings is completely normal and NOT a sign of heart stress?

options.A: A resting heart rate of 120 beats per minute
options.B: A regular resting pulse rate of 75 beats per minute
options.C: A blood pressure reading consistently above 140/90 mmHg
options.D: An apex beat displaced far to the left of the midclavicular line

explanation: A pulse of 75 bpm sits right in the middle of the normal 60–100 range. Nothing to worry about here! [learn more](GNS112_U6_T2#GNS112_U6_T2_h8)

question: When is the best time to record a patient's vital signs in their chart?

options.A: At the very end of the working shift
options.B: Whenever the physician asks for past notes
options.C: Only if the patient shows abnormal symptoms

explanation: Always document right away! Doing it immediately prevents mix-ups and keeps patient care safe and reliable. [learn more](GNS112_U6_T2#GNS112_U6_T2_h9)

question: Why is it crucial to quickly report abnormal vital signs to the doctor?

options.A: It ensures the hospital bed can be reassigned to another patient quickly
options.B: It proves the nurse completed all assigned tasks for the morning
options.C: It allows the healthcare team to intervene before the patient's condition worsens
options.D: It removes the need to monitor the patient for the rest of the day

explanation: Quick communication lets the medical team step in fast and prevent emergencies. Your quick thinking saves lives! [learn more](GNS112_U6_T2#GNS112_U6_T2_h9)
